payload.title: Prenup Requirements in Australia and Who Needs One
payload.audience: 30s, couples who are interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, 150k+ AUD budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a budget of AUD 150k or more, planning a destination wedding, who have heard the word 'prenup' and want a calm, plain explanation of what one actually is in Australia, when it can be made, what makes it binding, what it can cover, when a court can set it aside and how it sits alongside a wedding abroad, so they know what to raise with their own lawyers well before the wedding.
payload.goal: Speak with a Wedded Advisor: request a Wedded Concierge consultation at /wonderland-concierge so an advisor can plan the venue, travel, vendors and guest stays for the celebration abroad (the agreement itself, and all legal and financial advice, stays with each partner's own independent lawyer).
payload.angle: Page-one results for 'prenup' are mostly US-centric explainers and law-firm sales pages that use American terms, quote fees and blur advice with marketing. This guide answers the question only as official Australian sources state it, dated once as at November 2026: in Australia a prenup is a binding financial agreement (BFA) under Part VIIIA of the Family Law Act 1975, and the guide sets out when one can be made (before, during or after marriage, as the Act states), what makes it binding step by step (in writing, signed, independent legal advice for each partner with the signed statement, as the Act states), what it can cover, and when a court can set it aside, credited to the Act, the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, the Attorney-General's Department, Legal Aid and Moneysmart. It then covers who tends to consider one only as those sources describe the situations, and the angle page one misses for Australian couples marrying abroad: how a destination wedding and an agreement signed overseas sit with the Australian rules, stated only where an official source says so and otherwise 'ask your lawyer'. Calm, exact and general, with exactly one plain line that this is general information, not advice.
must_include: Intro with a direct answer in the first 100 words: in Australia a prenup is called a binding financial agreement under Part VIIIA of the Family Law Act 1975, and it is only binding if the Act's requirements are met, including independent legal advice for each partner [[VERIFY]], dated 'as at November 2026'. Exactly one plain general-information line in the intro (this is general information, not legal or financial advice; each partner needs their own independent legal advice, which is also a requirement for the agreement to be binding). Then exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways (a prenup is a BFA under the Family Law Act; it can be made before, during or after the marriage as the Act states; it binds only if the Act's requirements are met, including independent legal advice for each partner; a court can set one aside in circumstances the Act sets out).

What a prenup is in Australia: the binding financial agreement under Part VIIIA, the Australian term versus the everyday word 'prenup', and that the same framework covers agreements made during or after the marriage, credited to the Act, FCFCOA or AGD as sourced, with [[VERIFY]] until sourced.

When you can make one: before the marriage (section 90B), during (90C) and after separation or divorce (90D), only as the Act and FCFCOA state [[VERIFY: section numbers and descriptions]]; no timing advice beyond what sources say.

What makes it binding, as numbered steps: in writing and signed by both parties; each party receives independent legal advice on the effect on their rights and the advantages and disadvantages before signing; each receives a signed statement from their lawyer; original and copies handled as the Act states; not terminated or set aside. All as the Act states (section 90G as sourced), with [[VERIFY]] until sourced.

What it can cover: property, financial resources and spousal maintenance, and what it cannot override (for example child support or arrangements for children, only as sourced), credited to the Act, FCFCOA, Legal Aid or Moneysmart.

When a court can set one aside: the grounds the Act lists (for example fraud including non-disclosure, unconscionable conduct, impracticability, or a material change in circumstances relating to children, as section 90K states) in plain language, no case law, no advice, with [[VERIFY]] until sourced.

Who considers one: situations as official sources describe them (for example bringing significant assets, a business, inheritances or children from an earlier relationship, as sourced), framed as 'situations the sources describe', never a recommendation.

Destination weddings and agreements made overseas (a differentiator): how marrying abroad interacts with an Australian BFA and with an agreement signed in another country, only where an official source states it; otherwise 'ask your lawyer'. Links /expert-advice/overseas-marriage-certificate and /expert-advice/do-you-have-to-register-an-overseas-marriage-at-home rather than restating them. This section carries the ONLY Advisor line in the body, from brand-facts.md ('One Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact.' or equivalent brand-facts wording), tied to the celebration abroad, never the agreement, plus the /wonderland-concierge link (anchor 'Wedded Concierge').
Related paperwork links: /expert-advice/notice-of-intended-marriage, /expert-advice/who-can-perform-a-marriage and /expert-advice/name-change-after-marriage (drafts; link only if live at publish).

FAQ (4 to 6): What is a prenup called in Australia? Are prenups legally binding in Australia? Can you sign a prenup after the wedding? Do both partners need their own lawyer? Can a court set aside a prenup? Does a prenup signed overseas apply in Australia? Each answer from the same sources as the body; the overseas answer 'ask your lawyer' unless sourced.

Close: the one Advisor line from brand-facts.md (never the Wedded Advisor definition line or its closing phrase). Links /wonderland-concierge (Wedded Concierge) and /magazine as the magnet. UTMs utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=primary|secondary|magnet|closing on /wonderland-concierge and /magazine only.
avoid: Any legal statement not from an official source (Family Law Act 1975 on the Federal Register of Legislation, Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, Attorney-General's Department, Legal Aid commissions, Moneysmart) read live; undated claims.
Legal or financial advice, recommendations about whether a couple should have one, or tax, estate or asset-protection guidance; more than one general-information line; disclaimer stacking.
US terms and rules presented as Australian (for example 'prenuptial contract' state law, US court examples); case law commentary.
Any price, fee, cost of a lawyer or amount; 'free' or 'cheap'.
Lawyer, law firm, online-agreement service, financial adviser, vendor or bank names; directories of lawyers.
Foreign-country rules on prenups or marital property regimes beyond what an official source states; 'ask your lawyer' instead.
'Best' or ranking language; transfers, drive or flight times.
Anything implying the Wedded Advisor or Wedded Concierge helps with the agreement, lawyers, legal, financial or paperwork matters.

Wedded Privileges; Advisor claims beyond brand-facts.md; more than one Advisor line in the body besides the close; the Advisor definition line and the phrase 'last dance'; 'Wonderland Concierge' as anchor text.
Restating overseas certificate, registration or recognition detail that their own pages own.
Research talk in copy ('we could not confirm', 'according to our research'); per-line source credits; hedge stacking.
Competitor wedding sites, law-firm blogs, celebrity divorce stories or Wikipedia as sources; competitor wording or images.
Unromantic scare framing or divorce statistics; clichés, exclamation marks, keywords pasted in headings, em dashes, US spelling.
